newsitem.title: USA: Dollar mixed at US open, rises versus battered yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mixed at US open, rises versus battered yen.

text.p: The dollar moved higher against the yen overnight as investors continued to shun the Japanese unit in the wake of big currency losses in Southeast Asia, dealers said.

The yen again fell across the board amid concerns the broad devaluation of Asian currencies could derail Japan's fledgling economic recovery or force Japan to act to keep the yen weak in response, dealers said.
"Japan was having problems domestically, now they have problems in the region and that's more than enough to handle," said Jeffrey Yu, senior dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd New York.

Japan has pledged four billion dollars in financial assistance to Thailand as part of an International Monetary Fund baht bailout and investors saw that as a bad sign for a country already struggling with a prolonged slump.
"That may be small potatoes for a government, but the market perceives it as a problem that Japan has to pump out what little resources they have," said Yu.

The dollar opened at 118.42/52 yen, up from 117.78/88 at Thursday's close. Dollar/mark opened lower at 1.8355/59 versus 1.8390/00. The trade was consistent with mark/yen's rally toward a significant resistance point at 64.50.

The yen also suffered from declines in Japanese government bond yields, with the 10-year JGB reaching a record low at 2.065 percent overnight. That yield is a whopping 420 basis points below the 10-year Treasury note.
Asian players have sought better returns in the U.S. and other dollar-bloc nations, said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
"A lot of Asian capital is flowing to the high-yielders. People are concerned with JGB (yields) at record lows and they've got to look for some place to go," Refco said.
Dollar/mark failed to join the dollar/yen rally, checked by a continuing advance by mark/yen, dealers said.
The greenback fell below 1.83 marks in early U.S. morning trade after hovering near 1.84 as New York traders arrived.
Comments on Thursday from Bundesbank vice president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum continued to pressure the dollar, dealers said.
Gaddum was quoted in a German newspaper as saying the Bundesbank was concerned about rising consumer inflation and would keep its options open regarding possible shifts to variable-rate repo tenders.
"The Gaddum comments seem to be giving a very strong hint that the Bundesbank is prepared to raise interest rates if they have to and that's fueling gains for the deutschemark," said Malpede.

In other trade, the dollar was little changed at 1.5150/60 Swiss francs from 1.5158/63 at Thursday's close. Sterling rose to $1.5992/02 from $1.5910/20. The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3890/95 from C$1.3902/07. The Australian dollar opened at $0.7410/15, unchanged from Thursday's close.
